patient.name: Grace Osei
patient.complaint: Episodes of right upper quadrant pain after evening meals for 3 months
background: Lost 12 kg on a crash diet last year
Teaching assistant in Croydon; no allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with post-prandial RUQ pain in a woman with the five F's and normal bloods (biliary colic), or a stem that adds fever, jaundice or bowel obstruction to test which complication has developed.

points: Grace, 41, gets **RUQ pain after fatty meals**.
It comes in waves, lasts **1 to 3 hours**, then settles.
It goes through to between her **shoulder blades**.
She feels sick and once vomited; no fever.

steps.lead: Grace's story is textbook: **RUQ pain after fatty meals**, radiating to the back, lasting hours, with nausea.

visual.title: Where Grace's pain is
visual.caption: Biliary pain sits in the RUQ or epigastrium and radiates to the interscapular region or right shoulder.

steps.lead: Grace has almost all the **five F's** (female, forty, fat, fertile, family history) plus **rapid weight loss**.

points: Today, between attacks, her abdomen is soft.
No jaundice, no mass, no peritonism.

steps.lead: No fever, no Murphy's sign, no peritonism: Grace has **biliary colic**, a stone briefly blocking the cystic duct without infection. Most stones like hers are **cholesterol**.

visual.title: How long the pain lasts
visual.label: Grace 3 h
visual.caption: Pain lasting more than 6 hours is an emergency feature suggesting progression.

steps.q: Which new feature would mean Grace's stone has moved into her common bile duct and become infected?
steps.r: **Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain** (Charcot's triad) is ascending cholangitis. The other features fit simple colic or chronic disease.

steps.lead: Grace is safety-netted: **fever, pain over 6 hours, jaundice** or raised markers mean a complication. Each complication has a signature.

steps.text: **Pigment stones** in a young patient point to **chronic haemolysis** (sickle cell, G6PD deficiency), not the five F's.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' where the answer is abdominal ultrasound, and 'next investigation' questions where ultrasound is negative or the duct needs defining (MRCP).

steps.title: Grace's bloods
steps.text: All normal, as expected in uncomplicated biliary colic.

steps.q: Which test will confirm Grace's diagnosis?
steps.r: **Ultrasound** is the gold standard and first-line test for gallstones. Most stones are invisible on X-ray.

steps.lead: Grace's ultrasound shows **several gallstones**, a **normal wall** and no fluid: uncomplicated disease.

visual.title: Common bile duct diameter on ultrasound
bands: dilated: look for a duct stone
visual.label: Grace 4 mm
visual.caption: A normal-calibre duct and normal LFTs make a CBD stone unlikely.

steps.lead: Had Grace's scan been negative despite typical pain, or her duct dilated, **MRCP** would be next.

steps.title: Imaging pathway for suspected gallstones
nodes: Stones in gallbladder, normal duct → biliary colic
USS negative but high suspicion, or dilated duct → MRCP
Confirmed duct stone → ERCP to clear it
steps.caption: MRCP defines the duct; ERCP treats it.

steps.text: ERCP is **not** a diagnostic test here: it carries a risk of pancreatitis. Use **MRCP** to look, ERCP to treat.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where asymptomatic stones need nothing, colic gets an NSAID, and symptomatic gallstones get elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

steps.q: Grace calls during an attack. What is first-line analgesia?
steps.r: An **NSAID** such as diclofenac is first-line for biliary colic; opioids (morphine) if NSAIDs are contraindicated.

steps.lead: Grace gets **diclofenac** for attacks. Had her stones been found by chance with no symptoms, she would need **no treatment**.
Grace's stones cause symptoms, so she is listed for **elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy**.

steps.title: Gallstone management
nodes: Cholecystitis → IV antibiotics, fluids, early cholecystectomy

visual.title: Grace's attacks per month
visual.caption: Attacks escalate until the gallbladder is removed; cholecystectomy is definitive.

steps.lead: If Grace's stone causes a complication before surgery, each has its own emergency plan, and after surgery a **bile leak** must be considered.
Grace's pathway follows **NICE NG188**: ultrasound, analgesia, then laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic stones.

steps.text: Pain, fever and **bilious drain output** after cholecystectomy = **bile leak** until proven otherwise.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why cholesterol or pigment stones form, why colic hurts without infection, and why Crohn's disease or ileal resection raise gallstone risk.

steps.lead: Grace's stones are **cholesterol**: her bile carries more cholesterol than bile salts and phospholipids can dissolve. Rapid weight loss makes this worse.
Grace's pain comes from the gallbladder wall **spasming** against a stone stuck in the cystic duct. No bacteria are involved yet.
Grace has no bowel disease, but a patient with **terminal ileal Crohn's** loses bile salts and makes cholesterol stones for the same reason.

steps.q: Why does biliary colic not cause fever?
o: Bile is sterile at this stage, with no infection
steps.r: Colic is **transient obstruction and wall spasm** with no bacterial superinfection. Fever means cholecystitis or cholangitis.

mcq.q: What separates biliary colic from acute cholecystitis?
o: No fever, normal markers, negative Murphy's
mcq.r: Colic has **no inflammation**: no fever, normal bloods, negative Murphy's sign.

mcq.q: What is the most common type of gallstone?
Which stone type suggests chronic haemolysis?
mcq.r: **Pigment stones**: sickle cell disease, G6PD deficiency.

mcq.q: What does pneumobilia with small bowel obstruction suggest?
mcq.r: **Gallstone ileus**: a fistula lets a stone into the bowel and air into the biliary tree.

mcq.q: What is the first-line investigation for gallstones?
Ultrasound is negative but suspicion is high. What next?
What is the first-line analgesia for biliary colic?
What is the definitive treatment of symptomatic gallstones?

o: Milking the stone proximally and enterotomy
mcq.r: **Milk the stone proximally** and remove it via enterotomy.

mcq.q: Why does Crohn's disease increase gallstone risk?
o: Loss of terminal ileal bile salt reabsorption
mcq.r: Less **bile salt reabsorption** shrinks the pool, so bile becomes cholesterol-supersaturated.

technique.stem: A 42 year old woman has had three episodes of right upper quadrant pain in the past month, each starting an hour after a fatty meal and lasting about 2 hours. The pain radiates to her right shoulder and she feels nauseous. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and Murphy's sign is negative.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about RUQ pain: is there inflammation or not?
Post-prandial, self-limiting pain under 6 hours, no fever, negative Murphy's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Needs fever, constant pain and a positive Murphy's sign.
Needs jaundice and fever.
Chronic pancreatitis gives epigastric pain to the back, steatorrhoea, diabetes.
Ulcer pain is epigastric and linked to eating, not fatty meals and the shoulder.

steps.x: **C. Biliary colic.** RUQ pain after fat, settles within hours, normal bloods.

technique.stem: A 39 year old woman has right upper quadrant pain radiating to her right shoulder, mainly triggered after fried food. Her abdomen is soft and she is not jaundiced. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Stool antigen test for Helicobacter pylori

steps.x: A diagnostic investigation: which test shows the stones?

clues: right upper quadrant pain radiating to her right shoulder

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CT misses many gallstones and is not first-line.
Bloods are normal in colic and cannot diagnose stones.
That tests for peptic ulcer disease.
Most gallstones are radiolucent.

steps.x: **D. Ultrasound.** Gold standard and first-line for gallstones.

technique.stem: A 55 year old man has an abdominal ultrasound for abnormal LFTs from fatty liver. It shows two small gallstones in a normal gallbladder. He has never had abdominal pain. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his gallstones?

clues: two small gallstones in a normal gallbladder

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Surgery is for symptomatic stones.
No duct stone.
He has no pain to treat.
Dissolution is not standard.

steps.x: **C. No treatment.** Treat symptoms, not scans.

technique.stem: A 16 year old boy with sickle cell disease has recurrent right upper quadrant pain after meals. Ultrasound shows multiple small dark gallstones. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his gallstone formation?
o: Loss of bile salts in the terminal ileum

steps.x: A mechanism question: which stone, and why?
Young male with haemolysis and dark stones: **pigment stones**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No surgery is described.
Cholesterol supersaturation is the five F's mechanism.
That is the Crohn's or ileal resection mechanism.
Oestrogen affects women and cholesterol stones.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has had colicky right upper quadrant pain after meals for 2 months. Episodes last 1 to 3 hours and radiate to between her shoulder blades. She is nauseous during attacks. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. The site of her pain is shown (see item resources). Murphy's sign is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Post-prandial RUQ pain lasting hours with interscapular radiation, no fever, normal bloods and negative Murphy's sign is biliary colic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No fever, normal CRP, negative Murphy's.
Bilirubin is normal; no dilated duct described.
Reflux is burning retrosternal pain.
Ureteric colic is loin to groin.

practice.stem: An 81 year old woman with known gallstones has 3 days of colicky abdominal pain, distension and vomiting. She has not opened her bowels for 2 days. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Abdominal X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops and gas in the biliary tree.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pneumobilia with small bowel obstruction in an elderly woman with gallstones is gallstone ileus, from a stone passing through a cholecystoenteric fistula.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a bowel obstruction in a gallstone patient.

clues: 81 year old woman with known gallstones

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No jaundice; cholangitis does not obstruct the bowel.
Volvulus dilates the large bowel, without pneumobilia.
Ischaemia gives pain out of proportion, not biliary gas.
Perforation gives peritonitis and free gas, not pneumobilia.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man with G6PD deficiency has recurrent right upper quadrant pain after meals. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 120/72 mmHg. Ultrasound shows several small gallstones.
practice.q: Which is the most likely type of gallstone?
practice.e: Pigment stones are a strong marker of chronic haemolysis such as G6PD deficiency or sickle cell disease. Cholesterol stones fit the five F's.

steps.x: Stone type: who is the patient?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Calcium oxalate is a kidney stone.
Cholesterol stones fit the five F's, not haemolysis.
Cystine stones are renal, from cystinuria.
Uric acid stones are renal, from gout.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman with ileal Crohn's disease has had an ileal resection. She now has recurrent right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Ultrasound shows gallstones.
practice.q: Which is the most likely factor contributing to her gallstones?
practice.e: Crohn's disease and ileal resection impair terminal ileal bile salt reabsorption, so the bile salt pool shrinks and bile becomes cholesterol-supersaturated.

steps.x: A cause or risk factor question.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Azathioprine is linked to pancreatitis, not gallstones.
Hypercalcaemia causes kidney stones and pancreatitis.
No haemolysis described.
Low-fat diet does not cause stones; rapid weight loss does.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman with known gallstones has had several months of bloating, belching and upper abdominal discomfort after fatty food. She has no fever or jaundice. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a small, thick-walled gallbladder containing stones.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Flatulent dyspepsia over months with a contracted, thick-walled gallbladder containing stones is chronic cholecystitis. Acute cholecystitis gives fever and constant pain.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a longstanding gallstone problem.
Flatulent dyspepsia, chronic course, fibrosed gallbladder.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Acute needs fever and constant pain.
Empyema gives swinging fevers and a mass.
No bowel obstruction.
Mirizzi causes obstructive jaundice; she is not jaundiced.

steps.x: **B. Chronic cholecystitis.** Flatulent dyspepsia is its signature.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman has intermittent right upper quadrant pain after meals. She has no fever. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Ultrasound shows gallstones in the gallbladder and a common bile duct of 10 mm with a stone in its distal end.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A stone in a dilated common bile duct without fever or raised inflammatory markers is choledocholithiasis. Add fever and jaundice and it becomes cholangitis.

clues: common bile duct of 10 mm with a stone in its distal end
steps.x: Stone in a dilated CBD, no infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No fever; markers normal.
Mirizzi is a gallbladder neck stone compressing the hepatic duct.
A tumour, not a stone, would block the duct, with painless jaundice.
PSC gives beaded strictures, associated with UC.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has a 2 month history of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, radiating to her right shoulder. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Abdominal ultrasound is the gold standard and first-line test for gallstones. CT and X-ray miss most stones; ERCP is therapeutic.

steps.x: Initial investigation for suspected biliary colic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Most stones are radiolucent.
CT is not first-line and misses stones.
ERCP treats duct stones; it is invasive.
OGD investigates ulcers and reflux.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman has typical biliary-type pain after meals and mildly raised ALP. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Abdominal ultrasound shows no gallstones in the gallbladder, but the common bile duct is 8 mm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: When ultrasound is negative but suspicion remains, or the duct is dilated, MRCP is the next test to look for a duct stone before any ERCP.

steps.x: Next investigation after a non-diagnostic ultrasound.
High suspicion, dilated duct, negative USS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CT is less sensitive for duct stones.
ERCP is for treatment once a stone is confirmed.
HIDA assesses gallbladder function, not duct stones.
Delay with a dilated duct is unsafe.

steps.x: **D. MRCP.** Look with MRCP, treat with ERCP.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has an episode of colicky right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal. Ultrasound last month confirmed gallstones. She has no allergies, no renal or peptic ulcer disease and is not pregnant. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate analgesia?
practice.e: An NSAID such as diclofenac is first-line for biliary colic. Opioids such as morphine are used only if NSAIDs are contraindicated.

clues: no renal or peptic ulcer disease
steps.x: Biliary colic with no NSAID contraindication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Antispasmodic alone is not the notes' first-line.
Weak opioid, not first-line.
Opioid only if NSAIDs are contraindicated.
Paracetamol alone is usually inadequate.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has had four episodes of biliary colic in 3 months. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones with a normal gallbladder wall and a normal common bile duct. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 122/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Symptomatic gallstones are treated definitively with elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. ERCP is for CBD stones; cholecystostomy is for unfit patients with cholecystitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No duct stone.
Lithotripsy is not used for gallstones.
For unfit patients with cholecystitis or empyema.
Dissolution therapy is not standard.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman has small bowel obstruction from gallstone ileus confirmed on CT. She has been resuscitated with IV fluids and a nasogastric tube. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Laparotomy, milking the stone proximally and enterotomy
practice.e: Gallstone ileus is managed by laparotomy, milking the stone proximally and removing it through an enterotomy.

clues: small bowel obstruction from gallstone ileus
steps.x: Stone impacted in the small bowel.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Milk the stone proximally and remove via enterotomy.**

elim: The stone is usually at the terminal ileum, not reachable by colonoscopy.
ERCP cannot reach the small bowel obstruction.
Dissolution is far too slow.
No colonic disease to resect.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman with a BMI of 35 lost 20 kg in 4 months after bariatric surgery. She now has biliary colic. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a large, solitary, pale gallstone.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her gallstone formation?
o: Bile supersaturated with cholesterol relative to bile salts
practice.e: Cholesterol stones form when bile is supersaturated with cholesterol relative to bile salts and phospholipids; rapid weight loss is a recognised risk factor.

steps.x: Obesity and rapid weight loss; a cholesterol stone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bacterial deconjugation forms brown pigment stones in infected ducts.
Not the main gallstone mechanism.
Haemolysis makes pigment stones.
Conjugated bilirubin is soluble; pigment stones come from unconjugated.

prompts.q: What are gallstones and biliary colic, and what types of stone are there?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the stone type from the patient.

points.p: Gallstones (cholelithiasis): stones within the gallbladder
Most are cholesterol stones
Pigment stones mark chronic haemolysis (sickle cell, G6PD)
Biliary colic: temporary cystic duct obstruction, no infection
points.why: No fever, normal bloods, negative Murphy's.

prompts.q: What are the risk factors for gallstones?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: five F's plus bowel disease and weight loss.

points.p: Female, forty, fat, fertile, family history
Rapid weight loss
Crohn's disease and ileal resection
Chronic haemolysis (pigment stones)

prompts.q: Describe the classic presentation of biliary colic, and what makes it colic rather than cholecystitis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: timing and absence of inflammation.

points.p: RUQ pain after fatty meals
Radiates to interscapular region or shoulder
Lasts minutes to hours, with nausea and vomiting
No fever, normal LFTs/markers, no Murphy's sign, no peritonism

prompts.q: List the complications of gallstones and the one clue that identifies each.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each complication has a signature in the stem.

points.p: Empyema: swinging fevers, tender RUQ mass
Chronic cholecystitis: flatulent dyspepsia
Gallstone ileus: pneumobilia + small bowel obstruction
Choledocholithiasis: stone in dilated CBD
Ascending cholangitis: jaundice, fever, RUQ pain

prompts.q: Which emergency features tell you gallstone disease has progressed?

points.p: Fever
Pain over 6 hours
Raised inflammatory markers
Jaundice

prompts.q: How do you investigate suspected gallstones, and what next if ultrasound is negative?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: USS first, MRCP to look at the duct, ERCP to treat.

points.p: Abdominal ultrasound: gold standard and first-line
points.why: Most stones are invisible on X-ray.

points.p: Uncomplicated colic: stones, normal wall, no inflammation; bloods normal
USS negative but high suspicion: MRCP
points.why: Defines the duct or confirms clearance before ERCP.

prompts.q: How are asymptomatic gallstones, biliary colic and symptomatic gallstones each managed?

points.p: Asymptomatic incidental gallstones: no treatment
points.why: Treat the patient, not the scan.

points.p: Colic: NSAID (diclofenac) first-line
Symptomatic: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy

prompts.q: How are the gallstone emergencies managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one treatment per complication.

points.p: Cholecystitis: IV antibiotics, fluids, analgesia; acute lap chole or cholecystostomy if unfit
Choledocholithiasis: ERCP ± sphincterotomy
Gallstone ileus: milk stone proximally, enterotomy
Post-cholecystectomy pain, fever, bilious drain: bile leak

prompts.q: Why do cholesterol and pigment stones form, and why do Crohn's and ileal resection raise risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what is out of balance in the bile?

points.p: Cholesterol stones: bile supersaturated with cholesterol vs bile salts/phospholipids
Pigment stones: excess unconjugated bilirubin from haemolysis
Crohn's/ileal resection: loss of terminal ileal bile salt reabsorption

prompts.q: Why does biliary colic cause pain but no fever?

points.p: Stone transiently obstructs the cystic duct
Gallbladder wall spasm causes pain; no bacterial superinfection yet

glossary.gallstones: Hard stones of cholesterol or pigment formed in the gallbladder.
glossary.cholelithiasis: The presence of stones in the gallbladder.
glossary.biliary colic: Pain from a stone temporarily blocking the cystic duct, without infection.
glossary.cholesterol stones: The commonest gallstones, formed when bile carries too much cholesterol.
glossary.pigment stones: Gallstones made of bilirubin, typical of chronic haemolysis.
glossary.haemolysis: Breakdown of red blood cells, releasing bilirubin.
glossary.G6PD deficiency: An inherited enzyme deficiency that makes red cells break down under stress.
glossary.sickle cell disease: An inherited haemoglobin disorder causing chronic haemolysis and vaso-occlusive crises.
glossary.unconjugated bilirubin: Bilirubin not yet processed by the liver; raised in haemolysis.
glossary.five F's: Gallstone risk factors: female, forty, fat, fertile and family history.
glossary.cystic duct: The duct linking the gallbladder to the common bile duct.
glossary.CBD: Common bile duct, carrying bile to the duodenum.
glossary.Murphy's sign: Halted inspiration on RUQ pressure; positive in cholecystitis, negative in colic.
glossary.peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rebound and rigidity.
glossary.empyema: Pus filling the gallbladder, with swinging fevers and a tender mass.
glossary.chronic cholecystitis: Longstanding low-grade gallbladder inflammation causing flatulent dyspepsia.
glossary.flatulent dyspepsia: Bloating, belching and discomfort after fatty food.
glossary.gallstone ileus: Small bowel obstruction by a gallstone that passed through a fistula into the gut.
glossary.pneumobilia: Air in the biliary tree, seen on imaging.
glossary.enterotomy: A surgical cut into the bowel, used to remove a stone.
glossary.choledocholithiasis: A stone in the common bile duct.
glossary.ascending cholangitis: Infection of an obstructed bile duct: fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
glossary.Charcot's triad: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain, the classic signs of cholangitis.
glossary.MRCP: MRI of the bile and pancreatic ducts, used to look for duct stones.
glossary.ERCP: Endoscopic procedure to image and clear the bile duct; risks pancreatitis.
glossary.sphincterotomy: Cutting the sphincter of Oddi during ERCP to let stones pass.
glossary.laparoscopic cholecystectomy: Keyhole removal of the gallbladder; definitive for symptomatic stones.
glossary.cholecystostomy: A drain into the gallbladder through the skin, for patients unfit for surgery.
glossary.diclofenac: An NSAID; first-line analgesia for biliary colic.
glossary.NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as diclofenac or ibuprofen.
glossary.bile salts: Detergent molecules in bile that keep cholesterol dissolved; reabsorbed in the terminal ileum.
glossary.terminal ileum: The last part of the small bowel, where bile salts and vitamin B12 are absorbed.
glossary.bile leak: Bile escaping after gallbladder surgery; pain, fever and bilious drain fluid.
glossary.supersaturated: Holding more of a substance in solution than it can stably dissolve, so it crystallises.
